primaryCategory: "development"
description: "Learn how to lazy load comments section content with a real IntersectionObserver setup, load guard, and fetch pattern that cuts wasted network requests."
focusKeyword: "lazy load comments section"
takeaways:
  - "Most visitors never scroll down to comments, so loading them up front wastes bandwidth and main thread time."
  - "An IntersectionObserver on a placeholder element loads comments only when the section approaches the viewport."
  - "A simple load guard prevents duplicate fetches, because the observer can fire several times as a visitor scrolls past."
  - "Calling unobserve() after loading stops further callbacks, and the real test showed only 1 request after 3 more scrolls."
  - "Deferring a heavy comments script reduces Total Blocking Time, and a visible loading state inside an ARIA live region avoids a broken look."

<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">JavaScript</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Performance</span>
  </div>

  <p>Hi again! Today's build fixes a specific, very common performance mistake: loading an entire comments section, third party embed included, before a visitor has scrolled anywhere near it.</p>

  <p class="bx-lede">Ever loaded a blog post and felt the page stutter for a second while a comments widget somewhere far below the fold quietly finished loading? You never even scrolled there yet. A lazy load comments section fix is exactly what this guide builds, proven with a real network request count below, not just a claim.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="why-you-should-lazy-load-comments-section-content">Why You Should Lazy Load Comments Section Content</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A typical comments widget, whether homemade or a third party embed like <a href="https://disqus.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Disqus</a>, ships its own script, its own styling, and a network request for every comment thread, all before a visitor has read a single word of the article above it.</p>

  <p>Most visitors never scroll that far at all. Fetching and rendering all of that weight up front, for content the visitor has a real chance of never seeing, is exactly the kind of unnecessary work a good lazy load comments section pattern eliminates entirely.</p>

  <p>A long form article, a blog post, or a product review page are the three most common places this pattern earns its keep, since all three tend to place comments at the very bottom, well past the content most visitors actually came to read. A short landing page with comments close to the fold benefits far less, since there is little distance left to defer loading across.</p>

  <p>The savings compound across a whole site too. A single deferred request feels small on one page, but multiplied across every article on a busy blog, it adds up to a meaningful amount of bandwidth and script execution time that never has to happen for visitors who read one section and leave. A site publishing dozens of articles a month sees that saving repeated on every single one of them.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="watching-for-the-comments-section-with-intersectionobserver">Watching for the Comments Section With IntersectionObserver</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The same <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><code>IntersectionObserver</code></a> API used for infinite scroll and image lazy loading elsewhere on this site fits this problem just as well, watching a placeholder element and firing the moment it actually enters the viewport.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">observeComments.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">observer</span> = <span class="tok-kw">new</span> IntersectionObserver((<span class="tok-val">entries</span>) =&gt; {
  <span class="tok-val">entries</span>.forEach((<span class="tok-val">entry</span>) =&gt; {
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">entry</span>.isIntersecting &amp;&amp; <span class="tok-fn">shouldLoad</span>()) {
      <span class="tok-fn">loadComments</span>();
      <span class="tok-val">observer</span>.unobserve(<span class="tok-val">commentsEl</span>);
    }
  });
});
<span class="tok-val">observer</span>.observe(<span class="tok-val">commentsEl</span>);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Calling <code>observer.unobserve()</code> the moment comments actually load matters for a reason that is easy to overlook: without it, the observer keeps watching and keeps firing every time the section's visibility state changes, scrolling past it, back to it, past it again.</p>

  <p>Placing this placeholder element is worth a moment of care too. It needs to sit exactly where the real comments will eventually render, matching roughly the same height, so the page does not visibly jump or reflow the instant a lazy load comments section swap actually happens.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p><code>IntersectionObserver</code> has near universal support confirmed on <a href="https://caniuse.com/intersectionobserver" target="_blank" rel="noopener">caniuse.com</a>, so no polyfill or fallback is needed for a modern audience.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="guarding-against-a-duplicate-load">Guarding Against a Duplicate Load</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A real <code>IntersectionObserver</code> callback does not fire exactly once per element. It fires every time the intersection ratio crosses a threshold, which in practice can mean several calls in quick succession as a visitor scrolls past the exact same boundary.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">guard.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">createLoadGuard</span>() {
  <span class="tok-kw">let</span> <span class="tok-val">hasLoaded</span> = <span class="tok-kw">false</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">return function</span> <span class="tok-fn">shouldLoad</span>() {
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">hasLoaded</span>) <span class="tok-kw">return false</span>;
    <span class="tok-val">hasLoaded</span> = <span class="tok-kw">true</span>;
    <span class="tok-kw">return true</span>;
  };
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Without this guard, a fast scroll past the comments boundary can trigger the fetch call more than once before the first one even finishes, doubling up on a real network request for no reason. Six real observer fires against this exact guard prove the point clearly.</p>

  <p>This closure based pattern, a private variable captured inside a returned function, keeps the loaded state contained to exactly one comments section. A page with several independent comment threads, one per article in a list view for example, can safely create a separate guard per section without any of them interfering with each other.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Node.js output proving a load guard allows exactly one comments fetch even when the IntersectionObserver callback fires six times">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from guard.js, run against 6 real simulated observer fires.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="fetching-and-rendering-the-comments">Fetching and Rendering the Comments</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Once the guard allows exactly one load, fetching and rendering the actual comments is a small, ordinary async function.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">loadComments.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">async function</span> <span class="tok-fn">loadComments</span>() {
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">res</span> = <span class="tok-kw">await</span> fetch(<span class="tok-str">'/api/comments'</span>);
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">data</span> = <span class="tok-kw">await</span> <span class="tok-val">res</span>.json();
  <span class="tok-val">commentsEl</span>.innerHTML = <span class="tok-val">data</span>.comments
    .map((<span class="tok-val">c</span>) =&gt; <span class="tok-str">`&lt;p&gt;${c}&lt;/p&gt;`</span>)
    .join(<span class="tok-str">''</span>);
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Driving a real browser through the entire flow, page load, a real scroll to the comments section, then several more scrolls away and back, proves the whole mechanism end to end against a genuine local API endpoint rather than a mocked one.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Chromium output showing the comments API is called 0 times before scrolling, exactly 1 time after scrolling the comments section into view, and still only 1 time after scrolling away and back 3 more times">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Real scrolling, a real local API, and real request counting in Chromium via Playwright.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p>A comments section sitting 1600 pixels below the fold, roughly the distance used in the real test above, is genuinely never requested by the browser at all under this pattern until the visitor scrolls close enough to trigger the observer, not merely deprioritized or delayed.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="loading-state-and-accessibility">Loading State and Accessibility</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A blank box sitting where comments will eventually appear looks broken if there is no visible signal that anything is happening. A simple placeholder message, replaced the instant the real content arrives, fixes that cheaply, an approach <a href="https://css-tricks.com/lazy-loading-images-and-video/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSS-Tricks covers well</a> in a broader guide to lazy loading patterns.</p>

  <p>That placeholder also needs to sit inside an ARIA live region so a screen reader announces the comments arriving, the same accessibility gap covered for empty search results in an earlier guide applies here too, silent content changes are easy for a sighted visitor to notice and easy for a screen reader user to miss entirely.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="the-performance-payoff-what-this-actually-saves">The Performance Payoff: What This Actually Saves</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The real proof above already showed the core result: zero comments related network activity until the section is actually approaching the viewport, one request once it does.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead>
        <tr style="background:#2b2b2b !important;">
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Metric</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Loaded Immediately</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Lazy Loaded</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Initial page network requests</td><td>Includes comments widget</td><td>Excludes it entirely</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Main thread work on page load</td><td>Comments script parses immediately</td><td>Deferred until scrolled near</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Requests for a visitor who never scrolls down</td><td>Wasted, fetched anyway</td><td>Never fired at all</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>That reduced initial page weight has a direct line to <a href="/what-is-total-blocking-time-tbt/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Total Blocking Time</a>, since a heavy third party comments script parsing and executing during the initial load is exactly the kind of main thread work that metric penalizes.</p>

  <p>Measuring this properly means comparing a real before and after, the same page with comments loaded immediately versus the same page after the lazy load comments section change, run through the same throttled network profile in DevTools. The difference tends to show up clearly in both the initial request waterfall and the main thread activity track.</p>

  <p><a href="https://web.dev/articles/lcp-lazy-loading" target="_blank" rel="noopener">web.dev's guidance on lazy loading and LCP</a> makes the same case from the loading metrics side: deferring genuinely below the fold content, comments included, keeps the browser focused on what actually needs to render first. Google's own <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/page-experience" target="_blank" rel="noopener">page experience documentation</a> lists exactly this kind of deferred, below the fold loading as a legitimate technique for improving real user loading metrics.</p>

  <p>The benefit scales with how much a page relies on discussion to keep visitors engaged. A high traffic publisher running a lazy load comments section fix across every article page removes a fixed chunk of third party weight from millions of page loads a month, without touching how comments actually look or behave once someone scrolls down to read them.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-mistakes-when-lazy-loading-comments">Common Mistakes When Lazy Loading Comments</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Most lazy load comments section bugs trace back to one of these five gaps, each one easy to catch with a quick manual test against a page with real content above the fold.</p>

  <p>A useful check before shipping any lazy load comments section change is opening the Network tab, filtering to the comments request, reloading the page fresh, and confirming it stays empty until an actual scroll happens. That one manual pass catches most of the mistakes below before a visitor ever encounters them.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Forgetting the load guard:</b> a fast scroll can trigger the fetch more than once, proven above to be fixable with one small function.</li>
    <li><b>Never calling unobserve():</b> the observer keeps firing on every visibility change indefinitely, long after the comments have already loaded once.</li>
    <li><b>No visible loading state:</b> an empty box looks like a bug rather than content waiting to load.</li>
    <li><b>Setting the intersection threshold too close to the element itself:</b> the load only starts once the section is already fully visible, which a visitor can still notice as a visible loading delay.</li>
    <li><b>Testing only with fast local network conditions:</b> a comments fetch that feels instant in development can feel noticeably slow on a real mobile connection, worth testing with <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/network/reference" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chrome DevTools' network throttling</a> before shipping.</li>
  </ul>

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>Why lazy load comments section content instead of loading it upfront?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Most visitors never scroll far enough to see comments at all, so loading that content immediately wastes bandwidth and main thread time for a section that may never be seen.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>Does IntersectionObserver fire exactly once when an element becomes visible?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No, it can fire multiple times as the intersection ratio crosses a threshold repeatedly, which is exactly why a load guard is needed to prevent a duplicate fetch.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>Should unobserve() be called after the comments load?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes. Without it, the observer keeps watching the element and keeps firing on every scroll past its boundary, work that serves no purpose once the content has already loaded.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>Does this pattern work with a third party comments widget like Disqus?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, the same observer and guard logic can wrap loading that widget's script instead of a custom fetch call, deferring its entire weight until the section is actually approaching the viewport. A self hosted, open source alternative like <a href="https://github.com/giscus/giscus" target="_blank" rel="noopener">giscus</a> works the same way, and being open source, its own loading script can be inspected directly to see this pattern applied in a real production tool.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>How far below the fold should the observer trigger the load?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Close enough that comments feel ready by the time a visitor actually scrolls there, which the observer's rootMargin option controls by expanding its trigger boundary before the element is fully in view.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">6</span><span>Does lazy loading comments hurt SEO if a crawler never scrolls?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Google's crawler does render JavaScript and can trigger scroll based loading during rendering, but a comments section is rarely the primary content a page is trying to rank for, making this a low risk tradeoff in practice.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Comments should not load until scrolled near</h4><p>Real proof: 0 requests before scroll, 1 right after.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>IntersectionObserver can fire many times</h4><p>A guard function keeps the actual fetch to exactly one.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>unobserve() stops unnecessary future callbacks</h4><p>Proven above: 3 more scrolls, still only 1 total request.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>A loading state prevents a broken look</h4><p>An empty box reads as a bug without one.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>This reduces real Total Blocking Time</h4><p>Deferred script parsing means less upfront main thread work.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Works for third party widgets too</h4><p>Wrap the widget script load in the same observer pattern.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-cta">
    <h3>Ready to Trim Your Page's Below the Fold Weight?</h3>
    <p>This lazy load comments section pattern is a real, working starting point, an observer, a load guard, and a real API call, all proven with real captured output above.</p>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
